actions.name: Review vital signs flowsheet
actions.result: BP 120/85 mmHg, HR 76 bpm, RR 12/min, Temp 98.6°F, SpO2 99% RA (recorded at hospital discharge visit).

actions.name: Measure/confirm height and weight (self-reported via home scale, camera-guided)
actions.result: Height 5'2" (157 cm), Weight 145 lb (65.8 kg), BMI 26.1 kg/m² (overweight range).

actions.name: 24-hour dietary recall / usual intake pattern
actions.result: Patient reports: skips breakfast most days; large lunch (rice, dal, vegetable curry); dinner often after 8-9pm after work, sometimes includes seconds; frequent coffee with 2 tsp sugar x3/day; evening snacking on cookies or namkeen; occasional sugary soda.

actions.name: Weight history / recent weight change review
actions.result: Unintentional weight loss of 8 lb over past 3 months prior to hospitalization, consistent with uncontrolled hyperglycemia; weight now stable per patient report.

actions.name: Review HbA1c
actions.result: HbA1c 8.8% (goal <7.0%) — above target, indicates uncontrolled glycemia over past ~3 months.

actions.name: Review lipid panel
actions.result: Total cholesterol 210 mg/dL (H), HDL 38 mg/dL (L), Triglycerides 190 mg/dL (H) — pattern consistent with insulin resistance/metabolic syndrome.

actions.name: Review renal function labs (BUN/Creatinine)
actions.result: BUN 17 mg/dL (normal), Creatinine 0.9 mg/dL (normal) — no current evidence of diabetic nephropathy.

actions.name: Review total bilirubin
actions.result: Total bilirubin 1.2 mg/dL (upper normal) — not clinically significant.

actions.name: Review hospital discharge summary
actions.result: Discharge summary: first hospitalization for symptomatic hyperglycemia (polyuria, polydipsia, blurred vision, fatigue), started on insulin glargine 10 units at bedtime in addition to home metformin; diabetes education referral placed; outpatient follow-up with PCP and dietitian recommended within 1-2 weeks.

actions.name: Review current medication list and refill/pharmacy fill history
actions.result: Metformin 500mg BID — pharmacy fill history shows refills picked up roughly every 45-60 days instead of the expected 30 days, suggesting doses are being missed. Insulin glargine 10 units qHS — last refill was over 6 weeks ago for a 1-month supply.

actions.name: Diabetes distress / emotional readiness screen (brief check-in on coping)
actions.result: Patient endorses feeling overwhelmed, worried about complications, some difficulty sleeping; screen suggests elevated diabetes-related distress; recommend discussion with care team regarding anxiety management if it persists.

actions.name: Readiness-to-change / stage of change assessment
actions.result: Patient scores in contemplation stage: acknowledges need for dietary change but expresses ambivalence and uncertainty about how to implement it; appropriate approach is motivational interviewing rather than prescriptive advice.

actions.name: Review growth/weight trend chart
actions.result: Weight trend shows decline from ~153 lb to 145 lb over 3 months pre-hospitalization, now plateaued post-insulin initiation.

actions.name: Carbohydrate-counting knowledge/skill check
actions.result: When asked to estimate carbohydrate content of a sample plate, patient significantly underestimates portions of rice and chapati, indicating a knowledge gap despite her belief that she is 'tracking carbs.'

Hospital Discharge Summary
artifacts.author: Hospital Medicine Service
artifacts.body: 29-year-old woman presented with 2-month history of polyuria, polydipsia, blurred vision, and fatigue, found to have new/uncontrolled type 2 diabetes mellitus with HbA1c 8.8% and fasting glucose 185 mg/dL. No evidence of DKA on admission labs. Started on insulin glargine 10 units subcutaneously nightly in addition to home metformin 500mg twice daily. Diabetes self-management education ordered. Discharge instructions include follow-up with primary care within 1 week and referral to outpatient dietitian for medical nutrition therapy. Patient reports significant anxiety about diagnosis and new injectable medication.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient states she takes metformin but 'frequently forgets' due to long work hours, implying occasional missed doses but overall adherence.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Pharmacy fill history shows metformin refills occurring roughly every 45-55 days instead of the expected 30-day supply interval over the last two fill cycles, indicating a pattern of substantially missed doses rather than occasional lapses.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Self-reported adherence often underestimates the true gap between doses; pharmacy refill timing is an objective adherence proxy that should be reviewed and discussed non-judgmentally, especially when it conflicts with patient report.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient says she takes insulin glargine 'sometimes,' suggesting intermittent but ongoing use.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Pharmacy fill history shows the last insulin glargine pen fill was 6.5 weeks ago for a 30-day supply, with no refill picked up in the 2.5 weeks since it should have run out, suggesting she may currently be out of insulin entirely.
mismatches.teachingPoint: A gap in refill without a new fill can mean the patient has run out of medication entirely, not just missed occasional doses - this has direct implications for glycemic control and safety counseling, and should be explored with curiosity rather than confrontation.

objectives.text: Conduct a comprehensive nutrition-focused history (meal pattern, carbohydrate sources, beverages, barriers) sufficient to identify key contributors to uncontrolled glycemia.
Formulate an accurate PES (Problem, Etiology, Signs/Symptoms) statement linking excessive carbohydrate/sugar intake and irregular meal timing to elevated HbA1c and fasting glucose.

Apply motivational interviewing techniques to explore ambivalence, elicit the patient's own motivations, and avoid a prescriptive/restrictive approach given her contemplation-stage readiness and belief in strict elimination diets.
Identify and address real-world behavioral and cultural barriers (work schedule, family food traditions, time constraints) to generate feasible, patient-centered goals.

Integrate medication timing and action (metformin GI effects, insulin glargine hypoglycemia risk) with meal planning counseling, while identifying the adherence gap between patient report and pharmacy records.
Recognize hidden health literacy and emotional barriers (carb-counting fatigue, fear of being dismissed, guilt) that only emerge with rapport, and respond with validation rather than correction.

answerKey.primaryProblem: Excessive carbohydrate/sugar intake and irregular meal timing (nutrition-related) contributing to uncontrolled type 2 diabetes mellitus
differential: Carbohydrate intake and meal timing as primary nutrition diagnosis vs. medication non-adherence as primary driver (likely both contribute)
Diabetes distress/anxiety impairing self-management vs. purely knowledge-based deficit
Cultural dietary pattern itself vs. portion size/frequency as the modifiable factor
keyFindings: HbA1c 8.8% and fasting glucose 185 mg/dL, both above goal
BMI 26.1 kg/m2 (overweight), recent unintentional weight loss of 8 lb over 3 months pre-hospitalization
Dyslipidemia pattern consistent with metabolic syndrome (TC 210, HDL 38, TG 190)
Skips breakfast, large late dinner, high refined-carbohydrate and sugar-sweetened beverage intake, evening snacking
Pharmacy refill pattern suggests greater medication non-adherence (both metformin and insulin) than patient reports
Patient in contemplation stage with ambivalence, guilt about sweets, fear of restrictive diets, and belief that elimination diets are required
Hidden carb-counting attempts are exhausting and likely inaccurate, indicating unmet education need
plan: Document ADIME note: PES statement e.g. 'Excessive carbohydrate intake related to irregular meal timing and limited nutrition knowledge as evidenced by HbA1c 8.8%, fasting glucose 185 mg/dL, and reported skipped breakfast/large late dinners with frequent sugar-sweetened beverages.'
Use motivational interviewing to explore ambivalence about change; avoid prescriptive 'elimination diet' language; affirm her strengths (problem-solving, motivation, support system).
Collaboratively set 1-2 small, feasible behavior goals (e.g., consistent breakfast, swapping one sugary beverage, plate-method portioning for rice/chapati) rather than overhauling entire diet.
Provide basic, practical carbohydrate-counting/plate-method education tailored to her traditional diet rather than correcting her prior attempts harshly.

Coordinate with prescriber regarding the apparent gap between reported and actual medication adherence (pharmacy refill pattern) in a non-judgmental way; clarify she is not currently out of insulin without alarming her.
Address meal timing relative to insulin glargine dosing and metformin GI tolerance (taking with meals to reduce nausea).
Screen for and refer regarding diabetes-related distress/anxiety symptoms affecting self-management; coordinate with behavioral health as appropriate.
Discuss culturally respectful strategies for navigating festival/family meals (modified portions, timing, not framing as 'forbidden foods').
Schedule follow-up visit to reassess adherence, glucose logs, and progress on behavior goals.
redFlags: Possible unintentional insulin discontinuation (refill gap) with risk of worsening hyperglycemia - needs prompt clarification with patient and prescriber
Elevated diabetes-related distress/anxiety symptoms (racing heart, poor sleep, worry) that may impair self-management and warrant behavioral health follow-up
Recent unintentional weight loss history consistent with prior uncontrolled hyperglycemia - monitor weight stabilization
educationPoints: Type 2 diabetes is a multifactorial, progressive condition - not simply a failure of willpower.
Strict elimination of entire food groups (e.g., all rice) is not required; portion, pairing, and timing strategies can achieve glycemic goals while honoring cultural food traditions.
Consistent meal timing and not skipping breakfast can reduce large glucose swings and late-day overeating.
Pairing carbohydrates with protein/fat and choosing less-refined options can blunt post-meal glucose spikes.
Taking metformin with meals as prescribed can reduce GI side effects like nausea.
Understanding insulin glargine's basal action and hypoglycemia signs/management can reduce fear and support more consistent use.
Small, sustainable changes (one swap at a time) are more effective for long-term adherence than aggressive overhauls, especially during contemplation stage.

patient.name: Nisha Patel
patient.appearance: Joins the video visit from a tidy home office with a dual-monitor setup visible behind her; dressed in business-casual attire as if just stepped away from work; sits upright with tense posture, fidgets with a pen, has a notebook open with questions written down.

persona.personality: Intelligent, analytical, detail-oriented, but highly anxious and prone to overthinking; seeks control and certainty.
persona.communicationStyle: Asks many detailed, sometimes rapid-fire questions; may interrupt; wants justification for recommendations; can become overwhelmed and go quiet if given too much information at once.
persona.emotionalState: Anxious, fearful of complications, overwhelmed but earnestly motivated to understand and improve.
persona.background: Nisha grew up in a close-knit Indian-American family, earned a Master's in Computer Science, and now works long hours as a senior software engineer. She is married; her husband works long hours too but is emotionally supportive, and her mother-in-law often prepares traditional meals for the family. Outside of work she enjoys solving puzzles, reading sci-fi novels, and used to enjoy hiking before her schedule got busy.
speechExamples: Wait, can you explain that again? I want to make sure I actually understand it, not just nod along.
So if my HbA1c is 8.8%, what does that actually mean for my kidneys long-term?
I read online that cutting out all carbs completely is the only way to fix this - is that true?
I don't want to be one of those people who ends up on dialysis because I didn't take this seriously.
Honestly I feel like I should be able to figure this out myself, but I just can't seem to get it right.
concerns: Fear of developing complications like blindness or kidney failure
Concern about losing cognitive sharpness needed for her job
Uncertainty about whether she can keep eating traditional foods

She has been referred by the hospital discharge team for outpatient medical nutrition therapy. Review her chart before the visit.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Referral for nutrition assessment and counseling after first hospitalization for uncontrolled type 2 diabetes
scenario.openingLine: Hi... thanks for seeing me. I've been diagnosed with type 2 diabetes and I was just in the hospital for the first time ever, so I'm honestly still trying to wrap my head around all of this.
tasks: Complete a nutrition-focused history including meal pattern, carbohydrate sources, beverages, and any barriers to healthy eating
Review relevant labs, anthropometrics, and medication list with the patient

Use motivational interviewing to explore the patient's readiness to change
Collaboratively set at least one small, feasible nutrition-related goal and provide education

profile.title: First Nutrition Visit After Hospitalization for New, Uncontrolled Type 2 Diabetes
profile.summary: Nisha Patel is a 29-year-old anxious, high-achieving software engineer recently hospitalized for symptomatic, uncontrolled type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 8.8%), referred for outpatient medical nutrition therapy. The case teaches nutrition-focused history taking, PES statement formulation, motivational interviewing with a contemplation-stage patient who believes in strict elimination diets, and reconciling patient-reported medication adherence against objective pharmacy refill data.
profile.setting: Telehealth video visit, patient at home in her home office during a work break
profile.encounterType: Nutrition assessment and counseling (initial outpatient visit post-hospitalization)
